name: Betting against beta (low beta / low volatility)

origin.source_title: Betting Against Beta (Journal of Financial Economics)

how_it_works.simple: Calm stocks have done about as well as wild stocks, so buy extra of the calm ones and sell some of the wild ones.
how_it_works.analogy: Like noticing that the slow, steady horse finishes nearly as fast as the jumpy one, and backing the steady horse more heavily.
how_it_works.precise: BAB goes long low-beta assets levered to a beta of one and short high-beta assets de-levered to a beta of one, so it is market neutral. Frazzini and Pedersen's model says investors who cannot borrow buy high-beta assets instead, flattening the security market line; the effect appears in US and international stocks, Treasuries, credit and futures.

rule: Each month, estimate betas; rank stocks; build a low-beta portfolio and a high-beta portfolio weighted by beta rank; scale each to beta one at formation; BAB = low-beta portfolio minus high-beta portfolio (both in excess of the risk-free rate); rebalance monthly.
data_needed: Daily stock returns to estimate betas
Or the free AQR BAB factor dataset
economic_rationale: Leverage and margin constraints push constrained investors into high-beta assets, so low-beta assets earn higher risk-adjusted returns (Frazzini and Pedersen 2014).
why_it_might_fail: It needs leverage and shorting, and much of the paper return comes from small, costly-to-trade stocks; when funding tightens BAB returns are low, as the paper itself predicts.

reported_results.source: Frazzini and Pedersen, Betting Against Beta (May 2013 draft), Table III
reported_results.notes: Table III shows 0.70% per month excess return (annual_return is 0.70 x 12) and 10.7% annualized volatility; Fama-French 3-factor alpha 0.73% per month (t = 7.39). Gross of costs.

post_publication_evidence: In AQR's own updated series the US BAB factor kept a Sharpe ratio of about 0.71 from April 2012 to August 2026 (catalog computation), close to its in-sample level, though these are gross returns of a levered long-short portfolio. McLean and Pontiff (2016) find that across 97 published stock return predictors, portfolio returns are 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication (https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365).

relevance.reason: An equity and multi-asset low-risk factor; the same idea (low-beta currencies earn more per unit of risk) could be tested in FX.
